title: Ten days of cough with rusty sputum in a 60-year-old teacher
desc: This station involves a focused cough history and respiratory examination of a 60-year-old teacher seeing her GP. In Part 2 the candidate interprets her observations, blood results and chest X-ray report, diagnoses left lower lobe community-acquired pneumonia with a small parapneumonic effusion, assesses severity with CURB-65, plans outpatient treatment, answers her fear of cancer and safety-nets.
focus: Productive cough after a viral illness: a systems-based cough history and chest examination, then chest X-ray interpretation, severity assessment and outpatient management of community-acquired pneumonia
stem: You are a medical student on placement in a suburban general practice. Angela Green is a 60-year-old teacher who has come to see her GP with a cough. The GP has asked you to see her first.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mrs Green and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you her observations, her blood results and her chest X-ray report. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Angela Green, a 60-year-old secondary school art teacher. You feel tired, hot and generally unwell, and you cough now and then while you talk, but you can speak in full sentences. You are not of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander origin. When the candidate says what they would examine, the examiner gives the findings from the Exam findings below.

What the practice nurse reports (the examiner says this if the candidate asks for the observations taken at 09:40): "Temperature 38.3, heart rate 104 and regular, breathing 22, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, blood pressure 128/76."

Opening line: "I've just got this terrible cough that won't go away..."

The cough (give only when asked):

  • Onset: it started 10 days ago with a bad cold.
  • Character: at first a dry cough with a runny nose and sore throat. For the last 4 days you have been coughing up sticky, rust-coloured phlegm, about a quarter of a cup a day. It has no particular smell. No blood that you have seen.
  • Better or worse: nothing helps and nothing makes it worse.
  • Previous episodes: you have had colds with a cough before, but never anything like this.
  • Impact: you have not been able to teach for a week or play golf.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • Breathlessness: short of breath walking around the house. It gets better when you rest but does not go away completely.
  • Chest pain: a sharp pain on the left side of your chest for 3 days, worse when you breathe in deeply or cough. If asked how bad: about 4 out of 10, worse to about 6 when you cough.
  • Wheeze: you have noticed a wheeze.
  • Cold symptoms: the runny nose and sore throat have mostly gone.
  • General: you feel feverish, tired and unwell (malaise). No chills or shaking, no night sweats, no weight loss and your appetite is normal.
  • No calf pain or swelling.
  • No nausea, palpitations, breathlessness lying flat, waking at night breathless or ankle swelling.
  • No heartburn or reflux.

Context (only if asked): a few people at work have been sick. No recent travel, long trips, time in bed or operations. No dust, chemical or other exposures at work. No changes to your medicines. No lung disease or cancer, in you or your family. Your vaccinations are up to date.

Past medical history: high blood pressure for 20 years, well controlled on tablets. No operations.

Medications: perindopril 5 mg once a day (for years, unchanged), Panadol when you are unwell, and a vitamin D supplement.

Allergies: none known.

Family history: your mum had a heart attack 2 years ago and now has a pacemaker. Your dad died 5 years ago of a stroke, aged 87. Your sister has high blood pressure.

Social history: you teach art at a secondary school. You live with your husband Gerry, who is 61, and are well supported by him, your friends and your 3 adult children, who live nearby. You have never smoked. You have 1 glass of wine most nights. You walk for 45 minutes 3 times a week and play golf on weekends. You eat a varied diet. If asked your weight: 68 kg.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you thought it was just a cold that would pass, but it has gone on too long. Your real worry, which you say if the candidate asks what concerns you: "Could it be cancer?" You would like to know what is wrong and to get something to make it better so you can get back to work.

If asked something outside the script, give a realistic answer consistent with the story.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate says what they would examine):

  • General: looks unwell and flushed, alert and oriented to time, place and person. Speaking in full sentences with a mild increase in work of breathing. Mucous membranes slightly dry. No cyanosis. Weight 68 kg.
  • Vital signs (09:40 set): temperature 38.3 °C; HR 104 beats/min regular; RR 22/min; SpO2 95% on room air; BP 128/76 mmHg.
  • Hands and neck: no clubbing, no peripheral cyanosis, no tar staining. No cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy.
  • Respiratory: trachea central. Chest expansion reduced at the left base. Percussion dull over the left lower zone posteriorly and stony dull at the very left base; resonant elsewhere. Bronchial breath sounds with coarse inspiratory crackles and increased vocal resonance over the left lower zone; reduced breath sounds and reduced vocal resonance at the very left base. Scattered expiratory wheeze. No pleural rub. Right lung normal.
  • Cardiovascular: heart sounds dual with no murmur. JVP not raised. No ankle oedema.
  • Legs: both calves soft and non-tender, no swelling or redness.
  • ENT: throat mildly red, no exudate.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self as the medical student, confirms Angela's identity and gains consent for the history and examination.
Acknowledges the impact of the illness (a week off teaching, no golf), uses plain language and summarises back to her.
History
Characterises the cough:

kids.x: Onset and course: started 10 days ago with a bad cold, dry at first, productive for the last 4 days, unlike any previous cough.
Sputum: rust-coloured and sticky, about a quarter of a cup a day, no blood and no smell.
Aggravating and relieving factors (none) and the impact (unable to teach for a week or play golf).

check.x: Asks about breathlessness, chest pain and wheeze, and finds breathlessness walking around the house (better but not gone with rest), 3 days of left-sided pleuritic chest pain and a wheeze.
Asks about systemic features: fever, fatigue and malaise present; no chills or rigors, night sweats, weight loss or loss of appetite.
Asks about the context (at least two):
check.d: Source marking: full marks for at least two context questions (item 8) and screening questions from at least three systems (item 9); part marks for one context question and two systems.

kids.x: Recent cold and sick contacts at work.
Recent travel, immobility or surgery.
Occupational exposures.
Recent medication changes (e.g. ACE inhibitor).
Personal or family history of lung disease or cancer.
Vaccination status.

check.x: Screens other systems for differentials (at least three in total with item 6):

kids.x: Pulmonary embolism: calf pain or swelling.
Cardiac: palpitations, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, ankle swelling.
Gastrointestinal: reflux, nausea.

check.x: Past medical history: hypertension for 20 years, controlled on medication; no surgery.
Medications (perindopril 5 mg daily, paracetamol when unwell, vitamin D) and allergies (none known), so that an antibiotic can be chosen safely.
Family history: mother's heart attack and pacemaker, father's stroke at 87, sister's hypertension.
Social history:

kids.x: Smoking (lifelong non-smoker) and alcohol (1 glass of wine most nights).
Occupation (secondary school art teacher), home and supports (husband Gerry, 3 adult children nearby), exercise and diet.

check.x: Explores her ideas, concerns and expectations and draws out her worry that this could be cancer.
Examination
Asks for vital signs and identifies fever 38.3 °C, HR 104, RR 22, SpO2 95% on room air and a normal BP of 128/76.
General inspection: alert and oriented (no confusion), speaking in full sentences, mild increase in work of breathing, hydration (mucous membranes slightly dry), no cyanosis.
Hands and neck: clubbing, peripheral cyanosis, and cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes (all normal).
Examines the chest front and back and finds the left lower zone signs:

kids.x: Trachea central; reduced expansion at the left base.
Percussion dull over the left lower zone and stony dull at the very base.
Bronchial breathing, coarse crackles and increased vocal resonance over the left lower zone; reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance at the very base; scattered wheeze.

check.x: Cardiovascular and legs: heart sounds, JVP, ankle oedema, and both calves for signs of DVT (all normal).
Interpretation
Observations: persisting fever with mild tachycardia and tachypnoea, SpO2 95% on room air, normal BP and alert, unchanged between the two sets: stable, with no severity criterion met.
Bloods: neutrophilia (WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.6) and CRP 148 in keeping with a bacterial infection; urea 6.1 (not above 7) and normal creatinine.
Chest X-ray, read systematically:
check.d: Source marking: 1 mark each for general comments, left lower lobe consolidation, and loss of the costophrenic angle as an effusion.

kids.x: Comments on projection and adequacy (PA, inspiration, rotation).
Consolidation in the left lower zone, consistent with the left lower lobe.
Loss of the left costophrenic angle: a small left pleural effusion.

check.x: States the diagnosis of community-acquired pneumonia of the left lower lobe with a small parapneumonic effusion, linking the rusty productive sputum, pleuritic pain, fever, breathlessness and focal chest signs after a viral illness and sick contacts to the X-ray.

Gives at least two differentials, each with a reason against: pulmonary embolism (no travel, immobility, surgery or calf signs; clear infective picture with lobar consolidation), lung cancer with post-obstructive pneumonia (never smoked, no weight loss or haemoptysis, no mass or hilar abnormality; repeat X-ray at 6 weeks), acute bronchitis (focal signs and consolidation on X-ray).
check.d: Also accept heart failure (no orthopnoea or oedema, normal heart size, one-sided effusion with fever).

check.x: Names common organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), plus others such as Haemophilus influenzae, atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia (formerly Chlamydophila) pneumoniae, Legionella), Staphylococcus aureus (after influenza) and respiratory viruses.
check.d: Credit any three common CAP organisms including Streptococcus pneumoniae. Accept Haemophilus influenzae, Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia (formerly Chlamydophila) pneumoniae, Legionella, Staphylococcus aureus, Moraxella catarrhalis, Klebsiella pneumoniae or respiratory viruses (e.g. influenza).

check.x: Calculates CURB-65 as 0 (no confusion, urea 6.1, RR 22, BP 126/74 (latest), age 60), concludes this is low-severity pneumonia suitable for treatment at home, and discusses with the GP.
check.d: Accept CRB-65 0, CORB 0, or SMART-COP 0 on the available criteria, with the same conclusion.

check.x: Management

Recommends amoxicillin 1 g orally 8-hourly for 5 days (for the GP to prescribe) after confirming no penicillin allergy, and names doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days as the option if she were penicillin hypersensitive.
check.d: The source accepts amoxicillin for 5 to 7 days; credit any duration in that range. Critical element: confirms no penicillin allergy and gives correctly dosed amoxicillin; naming the doxycycline alternative is desirable but not required for the critical mark.

check.x: Supportive care: paracetamol 1 g up to 6-hourly (maximum 4 g a day) for fever and pleuritic pain, oral fluids for mild dehydration, rest, and a medical certificate for time off work.

Explains the diagnosis in plain words and answers her fear of cancer honestly: the X-ray shows a chest infection that explains her symptoms, and in a non-smoker with no weight loss cancer is unlikely, but a repeat X-ray will check that the shadow has cleared. Avoids false reassurance.
Safety netting

Gives red flags in plain words and where to go: call 000 for severe breathlessness, blue lips, confusion or collapse; see the GP the same day or go to ED for worsening breathlessness or chest pain, coughing up blood, a fever that is not settling, or being unable to drink or keep the tablets down.
Arranges GP review in 48 hours (sooner if worse) to check her response to the antibiotic, and states that not improving means reassessment (diagnosis, severity, change of antibiotic or hospital).
check.d: Desirable, not required for the critical mark: a persisting fever or a growing effusion raises the possibility of empyema and means hospital assessment with ultrasound.

check.x: Arranges a repeat chest X-ray in about 6 weeks with GP review of the result, to confirm the consolidation and effusion have cleared and to exclude an underlying lesion.

part2.lead: After you saw her, Angela had a chest X-ray and blood tests at the radiology and pathology services next door. She has come back to the practice this afternoon. Here are her observations, her blood results and her chest X-ray report.
part2.patient:
When the candidate explains, Angela asks, if not already covered:

  • "So it's an infection? Could it be cancer?"
  • "Do I need to go to hospital?"
  • "When can I go back to work?"

She is relieved by a clear, honest explanation and a plan to check the X-ray again. If told flatly "it's definitely not cancer" without a plan to check, she says, "But how can you be sure?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse on room air: at 09:40 on arrival and at 13:30 when she returned with her results. Weight 68 kg.
handover.model:
Read: temperature 38.3 then 38.0 °C, HR 104 then 100 regular, RR 22 at both times, SpO2 95% on room air at both times, BP 128/76 then 126/74, alert, pleuritic pain 4/10. No hospital chart is used in general practice, so judge these against the severity criteria.

For Angela: a persisting fever with mild tachycardia and tachypnoea, but her oxygen saturation is adequate on air, her blood pressure is normal and she is alert and unchanged over 4 hours. She meets none of the CURB-65 or SMART-COP criteria (RR below 30 and SpO2 above 90%, the SMART-COP thresholds for age over 50; SBP 90 or more and DBP above 60; HR below 125; no confusion).

What it changes: she is stable enough to be treated at home with close review. A drop in saturation, RR of 30 or more, low BP or new confusion would mean transfer to hospital.

rows.note: On arrival, before review by the medical student
Repeat set on return with results

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 11:10 at the collection centre next door; urgent request. No haemolysis.
handover.model:
Read: white cell count 14.2 with neutrophils 11.6 and CRP 148: a neutrophilia with a high CRP. Haemoglobin and platelets are normal. Sodium and potassium are normal. Urea 6.1 mmol/L and creatinine 58 with eGFR above 90 are normal. Albumin 36 is normal.

For Angela: a systemic inflammatory response in keeping with bacterial pneumonia. The urea is not above 7 mmol/L, so it scores 0 on CURB-65, and her kidney function is normal despite slightly dry mucous membranes.

What it changes: with the observations, her CURB-65 is 0 (low severity), so she is suitable for oral treatment at home. Normal renal function means no change to the amoxicillin dose and supports continuing her perindopril while she drinks well.

handover.label: Chest X-ray report
handover.result:
Examination: chest X-ray, PA erect. Angela Green, 60. Taken today at 10:57.

Clinical details: 10 days of cough after a viral illness, rust-coloured sputum for 4 days, left pleuritic chest pain, fever 38.3 °C. Non-smoker.

Comparison: none available.

Technical: slightly rotated (medial clavicular heads not quite equidistant from the spinous processes). Adequate inspiration with 8 posterior ribs visible. Good exposure.

Findings:

  • Soft tissues and bones: normal. No rib fracture or bony lesion.
  • Airways and mediastinum: trachea central. No mediastinal mass. Hila normal in size and position, with no hilar mass.
  • Lungs: airspace consolidation with air bronchograms in the left lower zone, consistent with the left lower lobe, with increased density behind the heart and loss of the outline of the medial left hemidiaphragm. Right lung clear. No discrete mass or cavity.
  • Heart: normal size. Left heart border clearly seen (preserved).
  • Pleura and diaphragm: the left costophrenic angle is lost, with a meniscus: a small left pleural effusion. Right costophrenic angle clear. No pneumothorax.
  • Lines and tubes: none.

Conclusion: left lower zone consolidation and a small left pleural effusion, consistent with left lower lobe pneumonia with a parapneumonic effusion. Follow-up chest X-ray in about 6 weeks is suggested to confirm resolution.
handover.model:
Read (DRSABCDE): correct patient, PA, adequate inspiration (8 posterior ribs), slightly rotated, well exposed. Soft tissues and bones normal. Trachea central, no mediastinal or hilar mass. Consolidation with air bronchograms in the left lower zone, in the left lower lobe: retrocardiac density and loss of the medial left hemidiaphragm, with the left heart border preserved. Heart size normal. Loss of the left costophrenic angle with a meniscus is a small effusion. No lines or tubes.

For Angela: this confirms left lower lobe pneumonia with a small parapneumonic effusion. That explains the rusty sputum, the left pleuritic pain, and the dullness and bronchial breathing at the left base. There is only one lobe involved and no cavity or mass.

What it changes: it confirms the diagnosis, so start antibiotics. Her small effusion does not need drainage now: blunting of the costophrenic angle alone is usually managed with antibiotics and close review. An effusion large enough to sample safely on ultrasound, or one that persists or grows (for example with a persisting fever), needs ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration (pH, LDH, glucose, Gram stain and culture) in hospital, to look for a complicated effusion or empyema. A repeat X-ray at about 6 weeks confirms resolution. This matters at 60, and it answers her fear of cancer.

ask: The GP has come back into the room. Please give an ISBAR handover of Angela to the GP, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, which organisms commonly cause it, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Angela now, here in general practice, including where she should be treated.
Angela asks you whether this could be cancer. What would you tell her, and what safety netting and follow-up would you arrange before she goes home?
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student. Angela Green, 60, teacher.
  • Situation: 10 days of cough after a cold, with rusty sputum for 4 days, left pleuritic pain and breathlessness. X-ray confirms left lower lobe pneumonia.
  • Background: hypertension on perindopril 5 mg. No allergies. Never smoked. Sick contacts at work.
  • Assessment: T 38.0, HR 100, RR 22, SpO2 95% on air, BP 126/74, alert and stable. Focal left basal consolidation signs with a small effusion. WCC 14.2, neutrophils 11.6, CRP 148: bacterial infection. Urea 6.1. X-ray (PA, adequate inspiration, slightly rotated): left lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms behind the heart, and a small left effusion (lost costophrenic angle with a meniscus). CURB-65 is 0, so low severity.
  • Recommendation: home with oral amoxicillin. Review in 48 hours. Repeat X-ray at 6 weeks. Please review her and prescribe the amoxicillin if you agree.

Most likely: community-acquired pneumonia of the left lower lobe with a small parapneumonic effusion. For it: productive rusty cough, fever, breathlessness, wheeze and left pleuritic pain after a viral illness and sick contacts. Focal left basal signs, neutrophilia, CRP 148, and the X-ray.

Organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common; rusty sputum is classic) plus two others, such as Haemophilus influenzae and an atypical (Mycoplasma pneumoniae).

  • Pulmonary embolism: against it: no immobility or calf signs, with a clear infective picture and consolidation.
  • Lung cancer with post-obstructive pneumonia: against it: never smoked, no weight loss and no mass. A repeat X-ray excludes it.
  • Acute bronchitis: against it: focal signs and consolidation on the X-ray.

1. Severity and setting: CURB-65 is 0 (no confusion, urea 6.1, RR 22, BP 126/74 (latest), age 60). Stable on an ABCDE assessment, so treat at home. Discuss with the GP.
  2. Antibiotic (eTG): no penicillin allergy, so amoxicillin 1 g orally 8-hourly for 5 days (source accepts 5 to 7). If penicillin hypersensitive: doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days.
  3. Supportive: paracetamol 1 g up to 6-hourly (maximum 4 g a day) for fever and pain. Oral fluids, as she is mildly dry. Rest. Medical certificate for time off work.
  4. Effusion: small, so no tap now.

• Honest answer: acknowledge her worry. The X-ray shows a chest infection (pneumonia) that explains all her symptoms. She has never smoked, has not lost weight and there is no mass, so cancer is unlikely. A repeat X-ray in 6 weeks will confirm it has cleared. Avoid a flat "definitely not".
  • Red flags: call 000 for severe breathlessness, blue lips, confusion or collapse. See the GP the same day or go to ED for worse breathlessness or chest pain, coughing blood, fever not settling after 2 days, or being unable to drink or keep tablets down.
  • Follow-up: GP review in 48 hours (sooner if worse); if not improving, reassess and consider hospital. Repeat chest X-ray in about 6 weeks with GP review of the result.

ddx.dx: Community-acquired pneumonia of the left lower lobe with a small parapneumonic effusion
ddx.for: Rusty productive cough, fever, left pleuritic pain and breathlessness after a cold with sick contacts, left basal dullness with bronchial breathing, neutrophilia with CRP 148, and left lower lobe consolidation with a small effusion on X-ray.

ddx.dx: Acute bronchitis or viral lower respiratory tract infection
ddx.for: Cough and wheeze following a cold, with sick contacts at work.
ddx.against: Focal bronchial breathing and dullness at the left base, CRP 148, and consolidation on the X-ray.

ddx.for: Left pleuritic chest pain, breathlessness and tachycardia.
ddx.against: No travel, immobility, surgery or calf symptoms; purulent rusty sputum after a viral illness, a neutrophilia and lobar consolidation.

ddx.for: Age 60 with a pneumonia, and her own fear of cancer.
ddx.against: Lifelong non-smoker, no weight or appetite loss, no haemoptysis, no lymphadenopathy, and no mass or hilar abnormality on the X-ray.

ddx.for: Breathlessness and a pleural effusion in a woman with long-standing hypertension.
ddx.against: No orthopnoea, nocturnal breathlessness or ankle swelling, JVP not raised, normal heart size, and a unilateral effusion with consolidation and fever.

guide:
Part 1 is set at about 09:45 in the GP's consulting room. When the candidate asks for observations, give the 09:40 nurse set, and give the other findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. For items 8 and 9, the source awards full marks for at least two context questions and screening questions from at least three systems (the respiratory questions in item 6 count as one system). In Part 2, which is set at about 13:30, hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Angela puts her questions while the candidate explains if they have not already been covered. Credit item 27 (organisms) if it is given in any Part 2 answer, usually the diagnosis question. Credit item 28 if the severity score comes up in any answer. Accept CRB-65, CORB or SMART-COP for item 28, and 5 to 7 days of amoxicillin for item 30.

A high-performing candidate characterises the cough and sputum and finds the pleuritic pain, breathlessness and wheeze. They screen for PE, cardiac and reflux causes, ask about smoking and weight loss, and pick up her fear of cancer. They examine the chest front and back and find the left basal signs. In Part 2 they read the X-ray systematically and name the left lower lobe consolidation and the effusion. They calculate CURB-65 as 0 and treat her at home with correctly dosed amoxicillin. They answer her fear honestly and arrange review at 48 hours and a repeat X-ray at 6 weeks.

A borderline candidate takes a cough history without context or other systems, examines only the front of the chest, or misses the effusion. They may give an antibiotic without asking about allergies, send a stable CURB-65 0 patient to hospital without a reason, offer false reassurance about cancer, or close with "come back if you are worried".
explain:
Diagnosis: community-acquired pneumonia of the left lower lobe

Angela has a classic bacterial pneumonia after a viral upper respiratory infection. A dry cough with coryza became productive of rust-coloured sputum (typical of pneumococcus). She has fever, malaise, breathlessness, wheeze and left pleuritic chest pain, and there were sick contacts at work. On examination there are signs of consolidation at the left base (dullness, bronchial breathing, crackles and increased vocal resonance). There are also signs of a small effusion below it (stony dullness with reduced breath sounds and vocal resonance). The X-ray shows left lower lobe consolidation with a small parapneumonic effusion.

A focused cough history

  • The cough: onset, duration, dry or productive, sputum colour, volume, smell and blood, what helps or worsens it, and previous episodes.
  • Context: recent viral illness and sick contacts, travel, immobility or surgery (PE; travel or residence in a high-prevalence country also for TB), occupational exposures, medication changes (ACE inhibitors cause a dry cough), personal and family lung disease or cancer, and vaccination status.
  • Other systems: respiratory (breathlessness, pleuritic pain, wheeze), PE (calf pain or swelling), cardiac (palpitations, orthopnoea, nocturnal breathlessness, ankle swelling), gastrointestinal (reflux, nausea) and constitutional (fever, rigors, weight loss, night sweats).
  • Social: always take a smoking history. It changes the probability of cancer, COPD and the follow-up plan.

Reading the chest X-ray

If time is short, state the key findings first, then work through the film systematically (DRSABCDE). Details: patient, date and projection. RIPE: rotation, inspiration, projection and exposure. Soft tissues and bone. Airways. Breathing (lungs and pleura). Cardiac. Diaphragm. Extras (lines and tubes). The left lower lobe lies behind the heart. Its consolidation causes a retrocardiac opacity and loss of the outline of the left hemidiaphragm. The left heart border stays visible in left lower lobe consolidation; if the left heart border is lost, think of the lingula instead. Loss of the costophrenic angle with a meniscus means a pleural effusion.

Assessing severity

CURB-65 scores one point each for: Confusion; Urea above 7 mmol/L; Respiratory rate 30 or more; Blood pressure, systolic below 90 or diastolic 60 or less; age 65 or over. eTG recommends clinical judgement supported by a tool that predicts the need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support, such as SMART-COP or, where bloods are not available, CORB (Confusion, SpO2 90% or less, RR 30 or more, SBP below 90 or DBP 60 or less). SMART-COP uses age-adjusted thresholds: RR ≥25 and SpO2 ≤93% at age 50 or under; RR ≥30 and SpO2 ≤90% over 50. CURB-65 and CRB-65 predict mortality and are widely used, and are accepted here. Any score supports clinical judgement and does not replace it. Angela scores 0 on CURB-65 and CORB, and 0 on SMART-COP for every criterion that can be assessed (arterial pH not measured), so she has low-severity pneumonia that is suitable for oral treatment at home.

Organisms

Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common bacterial cause. Others are Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis and Staphylococcus aureus (especially after influenza). Atypical organisms (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia (formerly Chlamydophila) pneumoniae, Legionella) and respiratory viruses are also common causes. Klebsiella pneumoniae is less common (alcohol misuse, diabetes, tropical northern Australia).

Differentials that matter

  • Acute bronchitis: cough after a cold, but without focal signs or consolidation. Antibiotics do not help.
  • Pulmonary embolism: must be considered whenever there is pleuritic pain and breathlessness. Here there is no risk factor or calf sign, and the infective picture is clear.
  • Lung cancer with post-obstructive pneumonia: her fear. It is unlikely in a non-smoker with no weight loss and no mass. Persisting consolidation on a follow-up film would raise concern.
  • Heart failure: no orthopnoea or oedema, and the heart size is normal.

Management (eTG)

  • Assess her stability (ABCDE assessment and vital signs) and severity, and treat at home if the severity is low and she can take oral medicines and fluids.
  • Low-severity CAP: amoxicillin 1 g orally 8-hourly for 5 days. With penicillin hypersensitivity, use doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days. Always confirm allergies first.
  • Paracetamol for fever and pleuritic pain, oral fluids if she is mildly dehydrated, and rest. If she cannot keep fluids down, consider withholding her perindopril until she is drinking again (sick day advice), and review her.
  • Review at 48 hours. If she is not improving, reassess the diagnosis, the severity and the effusion. She may need atypical cover or referral to hospital.
  • Parapneumonic effusion: a small effusion usually settles with antibiotics. Blunting of the costophrenic angle alone is usually managed with antibiotics and close review. An effusion large enough to sample safely on ultrasound, or one that persists or grows, needs ultrasound-guided diagnostic aspiration (pH, LDH, glucose, Gram stain and culture) in hospital. A persisting fever or worsening pain suggests a complicated effusion or empyema, which also needs hospital assessment.

Safety netting and follow-up

Explain the diagnosis honestly and address her fear of cancer without false reassurance. Tell her to call 000 for severe breathlessness, blue lips, confusion or collapse. She should see the GP the same day or go to ED for worsening breathlessness or chest pain, coughing up blood, a fever that has not settled after 48 hours, or being unable to drink or keep tablets down. The fever should settle within days, but the cough and tiredness can last several weeks. Arrange GP review at 48 hours and a repeat chest X-ray at about 6 weeks. The X-ray confirms that the consolidation and effusion have cleared and excludes an underlying lesion, which matters in patients over 50 or who smoke. Check that her influenza vaccination is up to date.
points: A productive cough with rusty sputum, fever, pleuritic pain and focal chest signs after a viral illness is community-acquired pneumonia until proven otherwise; Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause.
A cough history covers the cough and sputum, the context (sick contacts, travel, immobility, exposures, medication changes, smoking) and screening questions across at least three systems.
Read the chest X-ray systematically: left lower lobe consolidation sits behind the heart and hides the left hemidiaphragm, and a lost costophrenic angle with a meniscus is an effusion.
Assess severity with CURB-65 (or CRB-65 or SMART-COP) alongside clinical judgement: a score of 0 in a stable patient supports treatment at home.
For low-severity CAP, eTG recommends amoxicillin 1 g orally 8-hourly for 5 days (doxycycline if penicillin hypersensitive); confirm allergies first.
Review at 48 hours and repeat the chest X-ray at about 6 weeks in patients over 50 or who smoke, to confirm resolution and exclude an underlying lesion.
